content:
A sending church can pray, send money, open doors, and sit with you when the work is heavy. Those promises fade when they live only in a hallway conversation. This guide helps you and that church write a mutual support agreement: the help each side will give, how you will talk, when you will look at it again, and how the relationship ends.

This is a conversation, not a form to sign and not a second government for the plant. Notes from the meeting do not create an Everyfield login, a coach seat, or a right to read private notes. The app does not judge your calling, character, or fitness. If you later want a lawyer to turn the notes into something you both sign, that is a separate step. Everyfield does not supply that template.

---

## What this agreement is

Answer four questions. What help will we give each other? How will we communicate? When will we review what we promised? How does the relationship end?

Do not answer who has authority. If the question is who may hire, remove a pastor, hold the church's money, or set doctrine, stop. Open the documents that already name that authority for the plant and for the sending church. If those documents are unclear, say so. Do not hide an oversight clause inside a list of gifts.

The Launch Playbook expects the Senior Pastor to report to the elders. Core Group commitments include early elder partnership and fellowship with network churches. That is the plant's own life, not this agreement. [The three key documents](/wiki/core-group/commitment/the-three-key-documents) are covenants with people joining the Core Group. They do not settle support or an ending with a sending church.

| Question | Where it belongs |
| --- | --- |
| Help each side promises | This agreement |
| How you will talk, and how often | This agreement |
| A date to review the promises | This agreement |
| How either side ends the relationship | This agreement |
| Who may decide, hire, or discipline | Governing documents already in force |
| What Core Group members promise one another | The three key documents, later |

<Callout type="insight">
If no document names the authority, you have a gap in those documents. Fix it with the people who can amend them. Do not patch it here.
</Callout>

---

## Name the help on both sides

Both sides speak. A list of what the church will do for you, with silence about what you will do in return, is not mutual. Ask for sentences a stranger could check later.

- Prayer. Who prays, and on what rhythm.
- Money. Amount, how often it is sent, who receives it, and the date of the last gift.
- People. A team, a name you can call, or a room you can use, with dates.
- Mentoring. Who will meet with you, how often, and that this person is not a supervisor unless the governing documents already say so.
- Limits. What they will not do. A clear no hurts less than a hidden one.

Name your side too. Say how often you will update them, and what the update includes. Same-week news is a missed gift, a leader leaving, a moved launch date, or a conflict you cannot resolve in the plant. Do not let them hear that news first from someone else. If the plant already promised a church-planting contribution, do not invent a second percentage here.

Put sending-church money in the first-year budget as a named gift with an end date, and work that budget with your coach. [Finding a coach or mentor](/wiki/discovery/finding-a-coach-mentor) is a separate relationship. Hard questions do not make a coach an officer. Everyfield does not coach you in the app.

<Callout type="tip">
Write the number and the date. "We will support you as we can" is kind. It is not a promise you can review.
</Callout>

---

## Plan how you will talk

Name one person on your side and one person on theirs. If "the church" is the only contact, nobody owns the reply.

Pick a rhythm you will keep. Monthly fits many plants. Weekly may fit when money or a launch date is moving. A normal update covers Core Group progress, money received against what was promised, and one decision you need help thinking through. Leave out gossip and private care.

Say how you reach each other for same-week news, and what happens if the named person is away. You may tell a mentor, in person, how you and your household are holding up. That is voluntary. Do not require private notes, and do not treat a software score as a test of spiritual health. Those notes stay with the person who wrote them. No sending church or network receives them, and they are not in any partner report.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ."* — Galatians 6:2 (LSB)
</Callout>

Bearing a burden is personal. It is not a login.

---

## Put a review date on the calendar

Write a date both sides can keep before you need one. A date in the first year is usually soon enough to see whether the promises match real life.

Ask whether each side did what it named, whether a promise is now too heavy, and whether the launch date or budget should change the next promise. Ask whether authority questions are still in this agreement.

That last question is the risk of stopping at support. If the governing documents are clear, leave them alone. If they are fuzzy, say so and send the question to the people who can amend them. Do not add a line about who may overrule the Senior Pastor. Either side may also ask for an earlier review when a promise breaks.

---

## Say how the relationship ends

Write the ending while you still trust each other. Either side should be able to end it. Name the notice. Say whether unpaid gifts stop at notice, stop on a final date, or run through a short close. Pick one.

Do not invent a right to take back gifts or equipment already given. If a gift needs a condition, ask a lawyer or the sending church's treasurer to write it before the money is sent. This guide does not set tax treatment. Say what you will tell the Core Group, once you have one, and what you will not say in public. Ending support is not the same act as removing a pastor.

<Callout type="warning">
If the only plan is "we will figure it out," you will invent the ending during a fight. Write the notice, the last gift, and the public words now.
</Callout>

---

## Keep the agreement out of the app

This conversation does not grant access. Sharing is a separate choice.

If you start the plant yourself, sharing starts off. These notes do not switch it on. If a sending church or network invites the plant and you accept, you will see which categories start on. You can turn a category off later. That stops the sharing. It does not delete the relationship.

Private weekly check-ins are not a sharing category. No church or network receives them. Coach accounts are not part of the product. A mentor is a person you meet, not a seat. The app does not run background checks, handle your finances, or judge fitness. Do not write that the sending church may review your Everyfield account. If they want a report, send the update you already defined.

---

## Sit down and write the notes

Put both sides in the room. Read the notes back before you leave.

- [ ] People who will speak for each side
- [ ] Help the sending church promises, with amounts and dates if money is involved
- [ ] Help you promise in return, including how often you will update them
- [ ] What must be said the same week, and how you reach each other
- [ ] A review date
- [ ] How either side ends it, including notice and gifts not yet sent
- [ ] A line that authority stays in the governing documents
- [ ] A line that these notes do not open private notes or app data
- [ ] Whether a lawyer should review a written version

Write your own sentences. Do not paste another church's form or table. You may not have the right to use it. Do not let the side with the money write every line, and do not treat warmth as clarity. Elder authority, doctrine, and membership stay in their own documents. A coach's hard questions are not oversight.

If you cannot name the help, the talks, the review date, and the ending, you have a hope, not an agreement. Fill those four lines before you leave.

rulings: Bryan ruled R3 = Option A: "Mutual support agreement" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).
Wording call: kept the backlog title and suggested slug. The body uses Bryan's term mutual support agreement so partnership agreement is not read as a grant of oversight.

Wording call: no signable template and no default review interval. A document template remains a separate decision, and no source sets a review period. The article tells both sides to pick a date they can keep, often in the first year.

Wording call: addressed the planter as you, and told them to hold the meeting with sending church leaders in the room. Authority questions point to existing governing documents. The article does not assign a polity to the sending church and does not restate elder governance as a term of this agreement.

Wording call: product limits are stated in planter language, not requirement IDs. A self-started plant starts with sharing off. An accepted invitation shows categories that start on and can be changed later. Private weekly check-ins stay with the person who wrote them. Coach accounts, finance services, background checks, and fitness judgments are outside the agreement and outside the app.
